newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Turnaround seen for Asia market laggards - Invesco.
newsitem.headline: Turnaround seen for Asia market laggards - Invesco.

text.p: Some of the worst performers in Asian stock markets last year could surprise investors this year, fund manager Invesco said on Monday.
"Some of the really nasty surprises last year could turn into pleasant surprises in 1997," Anna Tong, chief investment officer at Invesco Asia, told reporters.

While Hong Kong is expected to continue leaping ahead on positive corporate earnings momentum and removal of a political discount, 1996 laggards such as Singapore, South Korea and Thailand should show some strength, Tong said.
"Given that Korea has digested so much bad news last year, any positive news this year may trigger some upside," she said.
On Monday, Seoul's KOSPI exchange closed 24.23 points or 3.49 percent higher at 718.46 on hopes of a political solution to recent labour unrest.
Throughout the region, corporate earnings seem to have bottomed out while valuations such as the price to earnings ratio are not demanding, Tong said.
Asia is also expected to benefit at the expense of the U.S. equity market, which Invesco considers overvalued by at least five percent, and a weak Japanese stock market.
"We don't necessarily see money flowing out of the U.S., we see new money going into other regions," said Rory Powe, Invesco's head of European equities.

In Hong Kong, Invesco holds a mid-year target for the Hang Seng Index of between 15,000 and 16,000, although an uncertain U.S. interest rate outlook and the British colony's transfer to China on July 1 could cloud the picture in the second half.

"(We feel) that on balance, the probability of U.S. interest rates moving up (is greater) than the probability of U.S. interest rates staying the same," Tong said. "In a benign inflationary environment...we are not expecting anything dramatic."

Invesco favours blue chips, particularly banks, and a number of red chips such as China Everbright International Ltd, China Resources Enterprise Ltd, Guangdong Investment Ltd and Goldlion Holdings Ltd.
"One of the key decisions this year will be when to cut back," said Tong. "We do not think now is the time."

In asset allocation, Invesco continues to overweight Hong Kong but has moved Singapore from underweight to neutral and will continue to buy on weakness to an overweight position on expectations of an economic recovery.
Malaysia is being reduced from an overweight position to neutral following an impressive 25 percent gain last year.

Tong said the Malaysian market soared on a narrowing current account deficit, which benefitted from the depreciating yen. Little further improvement is forecast, and while Invesco likes some of the mid-cap stocks, larger companies are under earnings risk.

"Forty percent of the market's earnings are derived from property, and we are already seeing some slowdown in the property sector," she said. The Philippines, which also surprised investors last year with a 19-percent gain, looks stretched at current levels but good value remains in some of the mid-cap stocks, she said.
Thailand will continue to underperform until the second half, Tong said.
"There is no way Thailand can achieve (the government's) seven percent growth forecast," she said. "This year we are looking for five percent."

At some point, the Bank of Thailand will have no choice but to widen its trading band for the baht against the U.S. dollar. This could cause some market capitulation, which should be used as a buying opportunity, she said.
